paras: The attempted lynching of Isaac Adkins took place at Fishkill, Dutchess County, New York, in December 1903, when a crowd of citizens prepared to hang Adkins, a 35-year-old Black man accused of attacking a 17-year-old white girl. The crowd bought a rope, tied a hangman's knot and chose a place of execution, but Justice Norris had Adkins taken secretly to the county jail at Poughkeepsie. Papers stressed that the attempt came within 60 miles of New York City, and one editorial cited it as proof that the North was as ready to lynch as the South.

According to the New York reports, Cora Wallace, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Henry Wallace of Fishkill, met Adkins on the street and asked where her father was working. Adkins was accused of leading her toward an old cemetery and attacking her in a secluded spot, until her screams drove him off and brought men to her aid. An armed posse, headed by Deputy-Sheriff Halight according to the Providence News, found him hiding in the woods near Brinckerhoff, about ten miles away, and brought him back for arraignment before Justice Norris.

As word of the charge spread, an angry crowd gathered outside the justice's office, with what the Providence News called "threats of vengeance on every side." One of Fishkill's "most prominent citizens" paid for a rope, another tied the hangman's knot, and a "committee" chose a spot for the hanging before the crowd started back for the office. Hearing the crowd, Norris broke off the examination, held Adkins for the grand jury and had officers take him out the back way to Poughkeepsie, so quietly that few people knew he had gone.

On the train Adkins repeatedly begged the officers to protect him from the mob. Henry Wallace, a Union army veteran, was kept by friends from going to Poughkeepsie to kill Adkins, and he was quoted as saying he had fought four years "to free the negroes, and this is my reward." Reports on Dec. 11 said threats of lynching were "loudly made" and that several citizens had volunteered to lead a mob to Poughkeepsie, but no report of a further attempt was found.

No report of an arrest or inquiry into the crowd appears in the coverage. A Poughkeepsie dispatch of Feb. 11, 1904, reported that "Isaac Atkins, a negro," had pleaded guilty to criminally assaulting a Fishkill village girl and was sentenced to five years at Sing Sing.

The fullest account appeared in the New York Evening World on Dec. 11 under the headline "Judge Saves Negro From Mob," and a longer version of the same story ran in the Providence News the next day as "Hangman's Noose Was Ready." Both credited the justice's "quick action" with preventing a hanging, while presenting the assault charge as established and giving the father's grief at length. A separate Newburg item, headed "Judge Lynch May Try Him," ran in the Waterbury Evening Democrat and the Bennington Evening Banner on Dec. 11.

On Dec. 12 the Jersey City News drew on the episode in an editorial attacking the Union League Club, writing that northerners had "no more love and far less sympathy" for Black people than southerners and were "just as ready to lynch him—as was shown at Fishkill on Thursday." The sentencing two months later reached print as a one-sentence wire item in an Ohio paper. All of the coverage found came from white dailies in New York, New England, New Jersey and Ohio; no report of the episode was found in the Black press.

The Providence News placed the averted lynching on "Wednesday afternoon," Dec. 9, while the Jersey City editorial said Thursday. The Providence News also said Adkins was jailed "for safe breaking," though its own story concerned only the assault charge, which the other reports and the later plea also describe.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Isaac Adkins
bases: A crowd at Fishkill bought a rope, tied a hangman's knot and chose a place to hang Isaac Adkins, a Black prisoner accused of assault, and was forestalled only when the justice had him taken secretly to the county jail (A1, A5); it is an attempted lynching with no one killed.

No one was killed: Adkins was spirited to the Poughkeepsie jail before the crowd reached him and was later sentenced in court (A1, A5, A7). The crowd acted without authority on the pretext of punishing an alleged assault on a white girl, so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching (A1, A5).

Two separate dispatches, a New York report (A1, A5) and a Newburg item (A2), agree that Adkins was jailed at Poughkeepsie on the Wallace charge amid lynching threats, and a later Poughkeepsie dispatch reports the sentence (A7).
